source.title: SAMformer: Unlocking the Potential of Transformers in Time Series Forecasting with Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Channel-Wise Attention
source.authors: Romain Ilbert; Ambroise Odonnat; Vasilii Feofanov; Aladin Virmaux; Giuseppe Paolo; Themis Palpanas; I. Redko

record.file_problem: Full paper text and appendix supplied; some figures and tables are flattened in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether optimizer choice and a sharpness-related property track the training–test gap in toy forecasting and real time-series forecasting. Its time-series regression setup and metrics differ from the catalog’s classification settings.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own toy and real-data findings about generalization, optimizer changes, and sharpness. The cited studies and their results are not recorded as rows. Some results are available only in figures, without recoverable numerical values.
record.test_reason: The study uses sharpness-aware optimization to improve forecasting and reports ordinary Hessian sharpness alongside forecasting loss. It does not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of training–test gaps. Its optimizer ablation concerns synthetic forecasting convergence, rather than V4's held-out comparison under limited tuning. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors attribute poor toy-task generalization mainly to attention trainability and sharp local minima, and report that SAM enables oracle-level toy performance and strong, stable real-data forecasting. They also emphasize channel-wise attention and the shallow architecture. These are their interpretations; the experiments do not establish V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates one-layer attention models on synthetic linear forecasting and real multivariate time-series forecasting, using validation/test MSE and Hessian sharpness. It does not use random-label classification, width sweeps, or the claim versions’ image and language benchmarks.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer and weight decay affect convergence in the synthetic task; the text reports AdamW sensitivity to weight-decay strength. SAM neighborhood size ρ affects test MSE, with larger values generally helping SAMformer. Initialization seed changes Transformer performance substantially. Dataset and prediction horizon define separate evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: The synthetic Transformer generalizes poorly; fixing attention partly improves validation performance, and SAM reaches oracle-level validation loss with much lower Hessian sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention training and SAM affect forecasting performance and ordinary Hessian sharpness in this synthetic regression setup.

fits_no_version.finding: SAMformer has lower Hessian sharpness on ETTh1 and Exchange and better, more stable forecasting performance than the Transformer baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM improves the tested shallow Transformer's forecasting performance and seed robustness, alongside reduced ordinary Hessian sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: Spectral reparameterization does not match SAM's improvements, and combining it with SAM adds computational cost without surpassing SAM alone.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectral reparameterization provides little benefit in the tested forecasting interventions.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD diverges, while AdamW either fails to converge or behaves similarly to Adam depending on weight decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer and weight-decay choices affect convergence on the synthetic attention-based regression task.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM neighborhood size affects forecasting MSE, and SAMformer outperforms competitors on seven of eight datasets overall.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed forecasting method's performance depends on SAM configuration and varies across datasets.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 235, 2024
record.problems: The central synthetic comparisons are conveyed partly through plots without recoverable numeric values. The real-data evidence concerns forecasting MSE and ordinary Hessian sharpness, so it does not directly validate V7’s magnitude-aware perturbation measure or the classification settings of the other versions. Some baseline values are taken from prior papers rather than rerun by the authors; the text identifies those sources.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result fitting the named settings of V1–V6 or V8 was found. Additional per-horizon values from Figures 8, 14 and 15 were not separately extracted where the supplied text did not provide recoverable numbers.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Test-error behavior as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out generalization under limited tuning on image or language benchmarks, including the stated recovery conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, small-data exceptions, underfitting, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: A change of application setting alone would not exclude a test. Here the decisive mismatches are the sharpness measure, outcome, and optimizer-comparison design. No version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label experiment or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD on the listed image-classification or language benchmarks; the paper compares optimizers on synthetic time-series regression.

The study measures Hessian sharpness and validation loss in toy and real time-series forecasting settings, but does not test magnitude-aware weight perturbations or compare the measure with norm- and margin-based measures.
No memorized-example identification, removal, or retraining experiment.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss and largest Hessian eigenvalue after training on the synthetic linear forecasting problem.

conditions.value: synthetic data generated with Eq. (2); L = 512, H = 96, D = 7

rows.measure: Validation loss relative to the oracle and sharpness relative to Random Transformer and Transformer + SAM.
rows.baseline: Oracle is the least-squares solution; Random Transformer is the fixed-attention comparison.
rows.value: Transformer has poor validation performance and a sharper minimum than Random Transformer and Transformer + SAM; λmax is ∼ ×104 relative to Transformer + SAM.
rows.note: The paper states that both transformer variants fail to recover Wtoy and that the standard Transformer converges to a sharper minimum. This is ordinary Hessian sharpness, not V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure.
rows.check: Largest Hessian eigenvalue and validation MSE do not establish V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship; partial is inappropriate.

rows.subject: Random Transformer
rows.size_stated: one-layer transformer; attention weights fixed; dm = 16
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss and largest Hessian eigenvalue after training on synthetic linear forecasting.

conditions.value: synthetic data generated with Eq. (2); L = 512, H = 96, D = 7

rows.measure: Validation loss and sharpness relative to Transformer and oracle.
rows.baseline: Transformer with trainable attention; oracle least-squares solution.
rows.value: Fixing self-attention alleviates the problem to some extent, but the model remains suboptimal; its loss landscape is smoother than Transformer’s.
rows.note: Attention weights are fixed at Glorot initialization; only W is optimized.
rows.check: Fixed-attention forecasting performance and ordinary Hessian sharpness do not measure V7.

rows.subject: Transformer + SAM
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss and largest Hessian eigenvalue after training on synthetic linear forecasting.

conditions.value: synthetic data generated with Eq. (2); L = 512, H = 96, D = 7

rows.measure: Validation loss relative to the oracle and sharpness relative to Transformer.
rows.value: Transformer + SAM generalizes perfectly to the oracle solution and has sharpness several orders of magnitude lower than Transformer; the paper reports λmax ∼ ×104 lower.
rows.note: The text says SAM achieves the desired solution in this toy experiment. This is an ordinary sharpness comparison, not V7’s magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
rows.check: SAM's oracle-level validation performance and lower Hessian eigenvalue do not establish V7's magnitude-aware correlation or comparative ranking.

rows.operation_detail: Compared test MSE across the neighborhood-size sensitivity sweep.

conditions.value: ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Electricity, Exchange, Traffic, Weather
ρ sweep; values shown in Figure 14

rows.measure: Test MSE sensitivity to ρ, compared with SAMformer.
rows.baseline: SAMformer at matching datasets, horizons and ρ values.
rows.value: TSMixer is less stable and fluctuates more; SAMformer’s MSE decreases smoothly with ρ and has less variance.

rows.note: This is a sensitivity result for the paper’s own model comparison, outside the claim versions.
rows.check: Neighborhood-size sensitivity is a method ablation outside the versions. Appendix C.2 describes greater TSMixer fluctuations, while Section 3.4 describes TSMixer as less sensitive to ρ; distinguish fluctuations from sensitivity.

relation.reason: Uses the sharpness–generalization rationale as a tool, without testing any named claim version.

tranche.reason: Uses sharpness-aware minimization to develop and evaluate a forecasting method. Hessian eigenvalues and forecasting MSE do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or ranking of training–test gaps; the optimizer ablations do not test V4's specified comparison.

source_check.notes: Figure 15's main caption misstates weight decays; R11–R12 correctly follow the subsection prose, legends and subcaptions. Appendix C.2 describes greater TSMixer fluctuations, while Section 3.4 calls TSMixer less sensitive to ρ; R13 accurately reflects the appendix.
